newsitem.title: USA: Dozens of inmates released from death row - study.
newsitem.headline: Dozens of inmates released from death row - study.

text.p: Nearly 70 inmates have been released from death row in U.S. prisons during the past 25 years because of doubts about their guilt, according to a study released on Wednesday.

The results of the study strengthened the American Bar Association recommendation on Monday that executions in the United States be halted until the judicial process can be overhauled, said Michael Radelet, chairman of the University of Florida's sociology department.
The ABA, citing an erosion of legal rights of death row inmates, called the appeals process in capital cases "seriously flawed" and said the death penalty discriminated against minorities.

Radelet, who compiled case studies of exonerations in death penalty cases along with academics at State University of New York and Tufts University, said he documented 68 instances of inmates who had been released from death row.

"The system regularly convicts and condemns innocent defendants," Radelet said. "Probably the most alarming thing about it is when you read these case studies, how lucky these people were to be exonerated."
"It makes you wonder how many people were not so lucky."
The inmate held the longest before exoneration was Mitchell Blazak, convicted of murder in Arizona in 1974 and released in 1995.

Another well-known case was that of James Richardson, who was convicted in 1967 of killing one of his children. He was exonerated and released from prison in 1989 following a reinvestigation of the case by then-Dade County state attorney Janet Reno.
Radelet said death penalty cases create great pressure on police, prosecutors and judges to arrest and convict someone, and consequently were more likely to have errors than other felony cases.
The ABA resolution was opposed by the U.S. Department of Justice, which said the current appeals process adequately protects the rights of death row inmates.
